**Support vectors are the observations whose constraints actively shape the optimum.** In the SVM dual representation, $w=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i x_i$. Points with zero multiplier contribute nothing to that expression. Points on or inside a soft margin may have nonzero multipliers, including misclassified points. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/svm.html)

Under an unchanged objective and exact optimal solution, removing constraints with zero multipliers can preserve the same optimum. The original dual solution remains available after deleting zero entries, and the same primal solution satisfies the remaining constraints. This explains why many distant, inactive points need not affect the fitted hyperplane.

**“Remove 90% and get exactly zero change” requires care.** If the implementation averages loss over sample count, removing points can change effective regularization unless the penalty is adjusted. Class weights may also depend on counts. Approximate solver tolerances and nonunique intercepts can alter the reported solution even when the ideal argument applies.

Do not label points inactive merely because they look distant in a plot; use the fitted margins and dual coefficients under the actual objective. A removed point might also matter after a later change in hyperparameters or features. Support-vector sparsity describes one fitted optimization problem, not a permanent guarantee that the rest of the dataset is unnecessary.

**Technical details and references.**

In the SVM dual, only examples with nonzero multipliers contribute to $w=\sum_i\alpha_i y_ix_i$. Removing examples known to have zero multipliers can leave the same optimum feasible and optimal under the same objective and constraints. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/svm.html)

However, the prompt's “zero change” needs qualifications: changing sample count can change effective regularization in average-loss parameterizations; numerical tolerances and nonunique intercepts can matter; and identifying non-support vectors from an approximate fit can be imperfect. Soft-margin support vectors may lie inside the margin or be misclassified.

Do not remove points merely because a heuristic says they look far away. Verify exact objective conventions and refit behavior, especially when class weights or per-example penalties change with the dataset.
